title: Xreal Built a Lighter, Comfier VR Alternative. Too Bad the Controls Are a Mess
description: Smart glasses company Xreal has released its magnum opus—the Xreal Aura, a $1,279 pair of extended-reality glasses that runs on Google’s Android XR pl
body: Smart glasses company Xreal has released its magnum opus—the Xreal Aura, a $1,279 pair of extended-reality glasses that runs on Google’s Android XR platform. The Aura glasses can project virtual screens into the wearer’s field of vision and include augmented-reality elements for use in the real world.The Aura glasses arrive just before the first wave of Android XR glasses from Google and Samsung, in partnership with glasses manufacturers Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. Those devices aim squarely at Meta’s smart-glasses empire. But the Aura glasses are more like virtual reality headsets, now in a more comfortable, glasses-like design. They go head-to-head with Meta’s VR Glasses, slated for release in early 2027.The first big caveat about the Aura glasses is that they’re wired. A long cord hooks onto the end of one of the glasses’ arms via a USB-C cable. That cord connects to an attached compute puck, about the size of a smartphone and weighing a little more than a half-pound. It comes in 12 or 16 GB storage options and has a battery that powers the glasses for roughly four to five hours with constant use.When the Aura glasses work, they’re wonderful. The glasses are pretty lightweight, at 95 grams. A four-mic array sits in the arms with Bose EQ tuning that sounds great. (You can also connect wireless headphones.) The display screen has a 1920 x 1200-pixel-per-eye resolution that is noticeably better than other Xreal glasses I’ve worn. A 70-degree field of view means the screens and virtual elements pop up in a wide frame of the wearer’s vision. That means the outer edges of your view will still be the real-life room around you. That can help if you’re trying not to fall over, but it can also be noticeable when trying to feel immersed in a movie.The big thing about Aura is that you can, in theory, run every app that already exists on Android. Xreal has a few primary categories for how it expects people to use its Aura glasses. The big one is entertainment. Like other Xreal glasses, the Aura can project a screen right in your field of vision. You can watch movies, TV shows, or YouTube videos, right in your field of view. The virtual screen stays fixed, or it can follow you around as you turn your head. You can also unplug the glasses from the compute puck and use them as display glasses to extend your Steam Deck’s screen, for example, though I had issues with that when playing more graphics-intensive games like Cyberpunk 2077.

title: I Found a Laser Hair Device That Doesn’t Look Ridiculous
description: Unlike straight LED lights, laser diodes provide collimated beams of light that travel in a straight line, allowing for more focused and intense treat
body: Unlike straight LED lights, laser diodes provide collimated beams of light that travel in a straight line, allowing for more focused and intense treatment of hair follicles. I actually saw some success with this treatment when I tested the HairBand’s closest competitor, Hairmax’s LaserBand 82 ComfortFlex ($849). It couldn’t help follicles that were scarred or had already died, but studies have shown that red-light therapy can energize follicles that have more recently become dormant.I did see some growth in the middle of my part with the LaserBand, and while I stopped using it to switch to the HairBand exclusively for the past five or so weeks, I admit this growth did make it difficult to isolate the HairBand’s contribution, especially since the headband’s coverage area is so small. Thus, the following observations are mainly on the wearing experience of the HairBand, not hair growth.Hold StillPhotograph: Kat MerckAt only 2 inches wide and five minutes per section, the HairBand took at least 15 minutes to cover my entire part, compared with the 3-inch-wide LaserBand, which also only needs to be used three times per week at 30 seconds per section for a total of 90 seconds. I’m a Type-A full-time working parent in my mid-forties, and let me tell you—15 minutes of doing nothing is a long time in my world.The HairBand has teeth and could sit on my head as long as it was in a normal headband position, right in the middle, but the weight of the battery pack pulls it forward ever so slightly, so if I was leaning over or doing anything that didn’t hold my head exactly straight, it would start to slip off. This meant I had to hold it with my hand, which meant no multitasking.Capillus’ marketing materials use words like “ritual” and feature pictures of twentysomethings admiring themselves in the mirror, but I can’t imagine these women are suffering from the perimenopausal hair loss that would necessitate use of a red-light device in the first place.I don’t consider myself to have an overly large head and have never had trouble with hats or other hair accessories, but this headband, which weighs only 6 ounces, felt quite small and somewhat precarious on my head overall. I should note it is also rather overtly feminine in style—my husband and I were able to share “custody” of the LaserBand, but he declined to wear this one, and I didn’t blame him.The $600 QuestionThere were two other concerns during my testing. One, a list of the box’s contents on the back mentioned quick-start instructions, but my box only had the headband and USB-C charging cord—no physical user guide to be found. There’s a QR code on the back of the box labeled “Capillus Protocol” that leads to the user guide, but its location and labeling are admittedly a bit confusing. Not that instructions are needed, since it’s pretty obvious how it works—push the start button on the battery pack, and it will beep and shut off when the five minutes are up.Two, this device is not currently FDA-cleared for treating hair loss or promoting regrowth. This isn’t ideal, but FDA-cleared is much different from FDA-approved; it simply requires the manufacturer to prove its product is “substantially equivalent” to an already FDA-cleared product. (And it doesn’t ensure results, just that it’s safe to use as directed.) Capillus’ rep tells me the brand is currently working on the FDA filing for the HairBand, which was released in September of this year, and intends to have it cleared in 2027. (The brand’s cap-style devices are FDA-cleared.) Even so, the HairBand is a unique device in this space, but if I’m spending that much on a red-light device, I would prefer a little more versatility in the design.Power up with unlimited access to WIRED. Get best-in-class reporting and exclusive subscriber content that’s too important to ignore. Subscribe Today.

title: Australia’s Plan to Manage Neil the Unruly Seal Involves ‘Hazing’ and ‘Seal Enrichment’
description: There is a 6-year-old elephant seal in Tasmania named Neil who has a taste for light property damage during the winter months. Now, the state has a ma
body: There is a 6-year-old elephant seal in Tasmania named Neil who has a taste for light property damage during the winter months. Now, the state has a management plan.Neil's annual “hauling out” and subsequent misadventures on the southeastern part of the island has delighted locals, making him a local mascot and a viral social media star.But Neil’s on-land hijinks—as he experiences his yearly “catastrophic molt,” during which he, like all elephant seals, sheds and replaces his top level of fur and epidermis— has also created headaches for local officials. Neil, who weighs over 2,000 pounds, has destroyed walkways, flattened bollards, bowled through fences, and rammed vehicles. The enormous and growing public interest in Neil has also been a source of concern, as officials spend tens of thousands of Australian dollars to keep the public at a safe distance from him.The Tasmanian government, finding itself in a precarious position, has finally decided to take action. The Department of Natural Resources and Environment published a 27-page dossier this week titled “Neil the Seal Management Plan.”“The purpose of this Plan is to set out a framework for managing the resident elephant seal known as Neil in Tasmania, recognising the complex challenges associated with his recurring haul out period,” the dossier states.Neil has a dedicated task force to monitor his whereabouts, and according to the dossier, they would take a “non-intervention,” hands-off approach if he hauls out in a secluded location. They’d keep tabs on Neil from a distance, erecting signs around the area to alert the public of Neil’s presence while advising them to keep their distance. Should the public tempt fate and approach Neil, the task force can call in security personnel to keep people and the seal safe.The second contingency plan is titled “on-site seal management,” which would be necessary if Neil comes ashore in a more public location, and has immediate access to roads and critical infrastructure that up the odds of molting-induced mayhem. One proposed management option involves “hazing,” which would essentially treat Neil like a frat pledge. The dossier doesn’t get into specifics—ostensibly there’s no paddling or eating a live goldfish involved—but highlights what it calls a “non-violent method of using deterrents and negative associations to disturb an animal, compelling them to move,” which can include “controlled visual, tactile and vocal stimuli where appropriate.”The document also notes that Neil appears to be adapting to and thus eluding “standard management practices,” meaning that the task force needs to stay nimble in coming up with new methods to curb Neil’s taste for antics.Tasmanian officials also propose “seal enrichment,” which they say would be used in tandem with other management options, to redirect “natural exploratory behaviors” (like engaging with infrastructure) toward decoy items “designed to withstand repeated interaction.”Officials also say that despite their best efforts to avoid Neil-related interruptions to daily life, “significant events,” such as road closures, public safety incidents, relocation or translocation activities, or wildlife-borne diseases, are still liable to happen. During such events, members of the public are advised to contact the Marine Mammal Hotline, also known as “0427 WHALES.”

schema.headline: Australia’s Plan to Manage Neil the Unruly Seal Involves ‘Hazing’ and ‘Seal Enrichment’

title: I Lived With the Apple HomeView for a Week. Here’s How It Went
description: Pressing and holding on the face of the HomeView allows you to customize your various “faces” (or remove them—it's a lot of options to have preloaded,
body: Pressing and holding on the face of the HomeView allows you to customize your various “faces” (or remove them—it's a lot of options to have preloaded, in my opinion, and I found myself swiping through too frequently to find the smart home page). You can also click on the plus button to add other faces or informational pages like weather and views of your home cameras. But that's all you can add, at least for now. There's no app store, but the device can reflect certain apps from your phone, along with general apps you'd find on an Apple device like Safari, FaceTime, Messages, Find My, Alarms, and more. I was surprised to see Spotify, Libby, and Yoto specifically ported over from my phone, but no other non-Apple apps have made it over so far, at least from my own collection of downloaded apps.Siri’s StrugglesPhotograph: Nena FarrellThere isn't a Siri AI app on the HomeView like on my iPhone, but the HomeView does use Siri AI to power its intelligence and answer your questions. You'll get a more conversational response than regular Siri, but I didn't find its answers to be that much more impressive. Siri ran into issues playing my music—it asks me whether the music should come from Books, TikTok, or Spotify if I don't specify, and then most of the time it still can't play the song on Spotify, even with my account set up. It also couldn't use Find My to find my iPhone when I asked. Both of these applications worked perfectly fine on the HomeView screen itself, but the on-device Siri isn't blowing me away thus far.In fact, most things worked better by touch than voice. Spotify voice requests didn't seem to work, but the Spotify app on the device worked fine, as did using the handoff feature to send Spotify music from my phone to the HomeView. The Find My feature also didn't work over voice command—when I called my phone the same name I had seen it referred to on the HomeView while playing music, it claimed I had no device under that name. However, tapping the Find My app on the HomeView let me find my phone in a list of devices and tap it to make it start going off. While I'm bummed Siri won't let me just voice-request it, I am thrilled to have a faster way to find my iPhone lost in my house than pulling up iCloud.com.I tested the HomeView with both an iPhone Air and an older iPhone 16 Pro, but you'll want a newer phone like the Air (or 17 Pro, 18 Pro, or iPhone Duo) to get the most out of HomeView and Siri, since that's what gives you access to the expressive, customizable Siri voices. Switching to my original phone left me stuck with a boring Siri voice that I can't customize like I could when using the iPhone Air. No matter which phone you use, you'll also need to update your phone's operating system to OS 27.2.1 in order to set up and connect to the HomeView (which also brings Siri AI onto your phone, much to my husband's chagrin).Touch and GoPhotograph: Nena FarrellThe main appeal of the HomeView, at least in my opinion, is the fact that it can control your smart-home devices with touch or voice. This is especially relevant since Apple is rolling out a larger smart-home ecosystem, with several devices coming later this year as part of its Apple Home Collection, including indoor and outdoor cameras, a smart thermostat, a video doorbell, a smart lock, and a couple of sensors. You can already control any Apple Home–compatible device on the HomeView, though, without needing Apple's lineup to release.

schema.headline: I Lived With the Apple HomeView for a Week. Here’s How It Went

title: Does Nvidia Got This? Interim CEO Colette Kress Says It’s Got This
description: Nvidia is going through it. The chipmaker’s iconic leader just resigned due to an international scandal, its stock has taken a hit, and it’s in a prec
body: Nvidia is going through it. The chipmaker’s iconic leader just resigned due to an international scandal, its stock has taken a hit, and it’s in a precarious position as it tries to maintain its dominance in the AI era.Following Jensen Huang’s ouster, the company’s interim CEO and still-CFO Colette Kress has been tasked with stabilizing the deck. So far, Kress’s public-facing duties have included running the company’s third-quarter earnings call and hosting an all-hands meeting for Nvidia’s money-hungry workforce. And as part of her calming campaign, Kress has also been deploying a catchphrase that sounds like it was taken straight from the draft files of a summer of ‘24 Democratic campaign strategist: “We’ve got this.”By WIRED’s count, Kress has publicly used the phrase three times in the past 24 hours, often putting emphasis or a little bit of zhuzh in it:Tuesday’s earnings call:“Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this.”Wednesday’s all-hands meeting:“Our ambition will not change. Our passion to innovate will not change. Our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change. We thank you all for the great quarter that we had. Just remember, we've got this.”Wednesday’s all-hands meeting, again:Kress ended Wednesday’s meeting by comparing Nvidia’s employees to “90,000 people packed into the sweatiest, hottest” University of Florida football game, all singing together.“It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony singing that song… Do you know what? We’re gonna hear that song, guys. And I believe in all of you that you will help sing it. But Nvidia, we’ve got this.”Kress’s new catchphrase perhaps isn’t the most inspiring; companies that got this usually don’t have to remind people how much they got this twice in one meeting. It’s a collectivist’s version of “You got this,” a slightly less corny version of “Yes we can,” a saying that may well pose more questions than it answers. (We got…what?)Nvidia investors, or any investor, might not have fist-pumped and said, “We’ve got this!” during a quick portfolio check these past 10 days. Anyone who has had the slightest hint of knowledge that Nvidia’s chips were finding their way into China is unlikely to be in a “We totally got this” mood at the moment.Still, some Nvidia employees appear to be inspired by Kress’s mantra. “Damn right we got this,” Aaron Erickson, Nvidia’s head of NemoClaw engineering, posted on X on Wednesday. Vega Shah, who works in portfolio management for Nvidia’s venture capital arm, shared Erickson’s post and echoed the phrase, adding her own rocket ship emoji to the post.And yesterday, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said the board did not intend to reinstate Huang, despite some calls on social media and within the company to put Huang back in the top spot.Which means that Kress, for the moment, has … got this.Paresh Dave contributed to this article.

schema.headline: Does Nvidia Got This? Interim CEO Colette Kress Says It’s Got This

title: Even His Own Officials Don’t Think Trump’s China Trip Will Lead to Progress on AI
description: Ahead of President Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping on Thursday, administration officials privately tell Inner Loop they see little room for pro
body: Ahead of President Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping on Thursday, administration officials privately tell Inner Loop they see little room for progress in alleviating AI safety and espionage concerns.As he departed the White House, Trump left it an open question whether he would press Xi on Chinese interference in AI or the Nvidia scandal, as part of what officials say is an effort to not antagonize China during the summit.But the fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, has made any negotiations around AI development fraught for the world's two largest economies, officials say.Back in September, the Trump administration moved to set up an AI incident hotline between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese vice premier He Lifeng to account for situations just like this one. Unfortunately, the communication channel remains at the concept stage and is not operational.Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters last week the US and Chinese governments had engaged in AI safety talks at a “technical level” since the hotline announcement, but admitted it was “still a work in progress.”Trump officials have previously discussed putting together a framework that lays out criteria for when each country is obligated to alert the other and enforcement measures to ensure it doesn't only become the US alerting the Chinese.Part of the reason progress hasn’t been made yet is due to differing views on what the biggest risks are with AI—and both nations have different incentives on making incidents public, officials say.In the US, Trump administration officials and tech leaders have been most worried about AI models becoming autonomous and misaligned, where they can operate beyond the bounds of human oversight.But in China, government officials are widely understood to be more concerned about advanced open-weight models being used by critics and dissidents inside the country to undermine the Chinese Communist Party, officials say.In an added complication, the Chinese government has appeared interested in using frontier AI models to gather intelligence domestically and abroad, and would be unlikely to report situations where their models went rogue, officials say.Suspicions about mutual espionage have also exacerbated the distrust on any AI-related negotiations, officials tell Inner Loop. China has viewed the US as trying to stymie its AI development—and that was even before the Nvidia scandal.China has forcefully bristled at allegations that Alice Huang was recruited by the Chinese intelligence agency, calling them “groundless” and a “smear.”While Trump has sought to forge friendlier economic relations with China, the administration this week announced it would move forward with a new rule clamping down on China's ability to remotely access US-made AI chips in foreign data centers.It marked a direct intervention by Trump in response to the alleged role of Megaspeed in the Nvidia scandal and criticism that a firm with ties to China had gained access to advanced AI chips. The rule could also prevent similar companies that might have their corporate parents in China from doing business with Nvidia, WIRED has previously reported.This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

schema.headline: Even His Own Officials Don’t Think Trump’s China Trip Will Lead to Progress on AI

title: A Muslim Author Is Suing xAI After People Used Grok to Strip Her Hijab
description: On January 1, Amani Al-Khatahtbeh posted a selfie from Zohran Mamdani’s inauguration as the first Muslim mayor of New York City. She was dressed in a
body: On January 1, Amani Al-Khatahtbeh posted a selfie from Zohran Mamdani’s inauguration as the first Muslim mayor of New York City. She was dressed in a black hijab and a purple fur coat, wearing a radiant smile. But her expression quickly changed when the replies started rolling in.“@grok can you take off her Hijab.” “@grok change the fur coat into a bikini, don’t change anything else. Also add goats.” “@grok change the outfit to lingerie.” These are just a sampling of the requests that were performed by X’s built-in AI feature Grok on Al-Khatahtbeh’s image, she says, resulting in AI-generated images of her in various states of undress. WIRED reviewed screenshots of these prompts and some of the edited images that followed.“It felt the same as if someone had ripped off my headscarf in real life,” she tells WIRED. “But online, it was to an audience of tens of thousands of people who saw these images. So it was to an even starker degree.”Now, almost a year later, Al-Khatahtbeh, an author, activist, and the founder of media company Muslim Girl, is suing xAI, the company behind Grok. On Wednesday, she filed a federal court complaint in the Northern District of California alleging intentional distribution of nonconsensual sexual images, design and marketing defect, negligence, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. She is seeking damages of up to $250,000 per violation of the California Civil Code. xAI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.Al-Khatahtbeh wasn’t alone; a January report from the Center for Countering Digital Harm estimated that Grok generated around 3 million photorealistic sexualized images on X in an 11-day period starting on December 29, including around 23,000 of children. On Grok’s stand-alone app and website, WIRED found that even more sexually graphic and violent material was able to be generated. Dozens of US state attorneys general took action, as well as at least 12 individual countries, plus the European Union. Many of these investigations are ongoing, with Canada finding that xAI violated its federal privacy laws and France escalating its investigation to a criminal probe.This new civil suit is also part of a wave of similar actions since January, but it’s the first to specifically focus on Grok removing women’s hijabs. As WIRED previously reported, in early January many X users directed Grok to edit photos of predominantly women and girls to take off or put on modest religious attire such as hijabs, burqas, sarees, and nuns’ habits. A review of 500 Grok images generated between January 6 and January 9 found that 5 percent of them contained these kinds of AI edits.“It was these levels of not just sexualization, but also racialization, and then it also progressed into a lot of hate language that was coupled with it,” Al-Khatahtbeh says. “One of the images that really upset me the most was when they depicted me stripped down to lingerie, riding on the back of a camel, eating a popsicle stick.”Her complaint argues that xAI was given notice of the trend of Grok targeting hijabi women and girls after the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), the largest Muslim civil rights and advocacy group in the US, called on xAI CEO Elon Musk to end “the ongoing use of the Grok app to allegedly harass, ‘unveil,’ and create sexually explicit images of women, including prominent Muslim women.” CAIR also connected the trend to existing hostile attitudes toward “Islam, Muslims, and political causes widely supported by Muslims, such as Palestinian freedom.”This is all too familiar to Al-Khatahtbeh, who typically goes by her first name to hundreds of thousands of social media followers. In the replies to her selfie at Mamdani’s inauguration, in addition to prompting Grok to “put her in a burqa” and other commands, dozens of replies contained violent, anti-Muslim sentiment.Al-Khatahtbeh says the internet feels more hostile to Muslim women and girls than when she first launched her media platform more than a decade ago. “People have been equipped with more advanced ways to exercise their hate,” she says.When the AI abuse started in January, Al-Khatahtbeh didn’t know what to do. So she called 911, and when officers arrived at her apartment, she says she showed them the photos that were being generated of her on X. They took a report, but told her they couldn’t do anything about it. Meanwhile, she reported the images on X, but she says they weren’t taken down immediately. In the days following the scrutiny over Grok’s nudification capabilities, xAI limited the ability to use these tools to paying subscribers only. But that didn’t stop the sexualized images from being created, it just meant users had to pay xAI to make them.After confiding with women in her community, one encouraged Al-Khatahtbeh to pursue a lawsuit. Now she’s being represented by Hillary Nappi, who leads a sexual-assault practice group and has worked on amicus briefs regarding sexual exploitation on Twitter before Musk renamed it X. Nappi’s strategy in this case includes using defective product law to assert that xAI designed Grok to sexually exploit women and children. It’s a strategy that has increasingly been leveraged against big tech companies like Meta and Google to find them liable for negligent product design that harms young users.“The only way you get some change against Big Tech is to sue them,” Nappi tells WIRED. “Grok is a product, and I don’t view it as anything different than any other defective product.”In this case, Al-Khatahtbeh’s complaint asserts that xAI could and should have designed Grok to prevent users from being able to prompt the removal of religious garments like the hijab in images depicting real people. It also says Grok shouldn’t have been able to create and post “sexualized depictions of identifiable, non-consenting real people” in general.“Because models of this kind are trained on large, uncurated image datasets, garments such as hijabs, abayas, sarees, and other modest religious dress are readily recognizable to the model, and a prompt directing their removal is trivially easy to execute unless the system is designed to refuse it,” the complaint says.This kind of violation at the intersection of her identity as a Muslim and a woman is what Al-Khatahtbeh says motivated her to speak out, with the hope that she can make the internet safer for women and girls in her community.“It does take the harm to a higher level for someone like me,” she says. “These faceless users on X shouldn’t have the ability to hop on and violate a woman on the other side of the country in this way.”

schema.headline: A Muslim Author Is Suing xAI After People Used Grok to Strip Her Hijab

title: ‘The Predators Are Real’: Senate Hearing Slams Roblox Over Child Sex Abuse
description: People who say they were groomed on Roblox testified in front of a Congressional subcommittee Tuesday about safety risks associated with the popular g
body: People who say they were groomed on Roblox testified in front of a Congressional subcommittee Tuesday about safety risks associated with the popular gaming platform frequented by kids and teenagers.“Roblox is one of the most popular gaming platforms in the world,” Republican senator Josh Hawley said in his opening remarks. “If your children are on Roblox they are being exposed in all likelihood to sexual predators … to sexually exploitative content, left, right, and center.”The hearing was intended to address the bipartisan legislation introduced by Hawley and Democratic senator Dick Durbin, coauthors of the No Forced Arbitration for Child Sexual Exploitation and Cyber Injuries Act, which would allow families of victims to sue Roblox directly instead of being forced to settle their claims privately in arbitration, as the platform’s terms of service currently dictate.The process of forced arbitration “strips consumers and workers of their rights,” testified Myriam Gilles, a law professor at Northwestern University who is an expert on forced arbitration. “I never expected to come before this body to talk about its use against 9-year-olds, but that’s where we are.”Roblox is currently facing nearly 200 lawsuits from families who allege that their children were groomed by sexual predators posing as children on the platform. According to Hawley, Roblox CEO David Baszucki was invited to testify at the hearing but declined.“He may think he’s silent, but in fact he’s testifying, and what he’s testifying to is his commitment to money over people,” Hawley said.In a statement, Nicky Jackson Colaço, global head of public policy at Roblox, told WIRED, “Safety has been central to Roblox since we launched. We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat. A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety. Protecting children online takes stronger protections, better tools, and consistent standards that apply everywhere kids spend time online.”Roblox has previously argued that users waive their right to sue in open court in the platform’s terms of agreement. According to Roblox’s own data, 35 percent of its age-checked daily active users are under the age of 13—too young to fully comprehend the terms of the agreement, witnesses argued.“There is no way an 8-year-old could read those terms and then sign away their right to a moment in court, effectively silencing themselves,” Republican senator Katie Britt said after being presented with a copy of the multi-page agreement.Two of those who testified before Congress were alleged survivors of grooming on the platform. One was Michael Schlep, a content creator who has advocated for more stringent child safety measures on the platform.Schlep testified that when he was 12, he met a game developer on the platform who befriended him in a public chatroom, then moved to private chats. He alleges he was exposed to “violent pornography, cartel beheadings, and extreme racist ideologies” that he says was a result of his communication with this adult man, and that his abuser exposed his private information, leading to a suicide attempt. He currently runs a YouTube channel exposing alleged Roblox child predators and criticizing the platform for failing to protect children, which has led to Roblox hitting him with a cease-and-desist.“Roblox must be held accountable publicly,” Schlep testified. “They will not voluntarily act to protect children.”The hearing also featured testimony from a Marine Corps veteran identified as Woody Doe, who alleged that he was groomed, then sexually assaulted by an adult man he met on Roblox when he was 11 years old. “For years, I carried the shame of what happened,” he testified. He now has a lawsuit pending against Roblox for allegedly failing to warn parents and children of the dangers of the platform.“I cannot go back and protect the 11-year-old boy I once was, but I can speak for him today … and prevent any other children from ever experiencing the same pain,” he said.Roblox is a massive gaming platform, with about 138 million daily active users according to recent company data. As of 2025, 39.7 million daily active users were under the age of 13.In response to the litigation and to intense media scrutiny, Roblox has adopted what it says are more stringent child-safety measures, including AI-assisted face recognition to estimate a user’s age. But Khari James, senior legal counsel at the National Center on Sexual Exploitation said face-recognition technology isn’t always accurate, and predators could potentially purchase verified accounts to continue to prey on children. Doing face verifications just once, she argues, gives predators “complete access to all the children on Roblox.”“Roblox may be a virtual world, but the children are real,” James said during her testimony. “The predators are real. The addiction is real. The exploitation is real, and the consequences are real. Children should never have to enter a game marketed to them and wonder whether the person on the other side of the screen is there to play with them or prey on them.”Update, November 17 at 9 pm: The story was updated to correct name and title of the Roblox spokesperson who provided comment.

schema.headline: ‘The Predators Are Real’: Senate Hearing Slams Roblox Over Child Sex Abuse

title: Voyager 1 Beat the Odds and Is Still Working a Light-Day Away From Earth
description: One of NASA’s longest-tenured spacecraft is quite literally stuck in the past.Voyager 1, launched in September 1977 toward the outer planets of our so
body: One of NASA’s longest-tenured spacecraft is quite literally stuck in the past.Voyager 1, launched in September 1977 toward the outer planets of our solar system, achieved a historic milestone on Wednesday: It became the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth. The spacecraft is so far away, that by the time its light reaches Earth, it comes from the spacecraft as it existed one day in the past. The achievement is one researchers hadn’t planned on, and yet, as Voyager 1 wades deeper into uncharted stretches of the galaxy, it continues sending back valuable scientific information.“It's just a wonderful happenstance,” Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, says of the milestone. “Just as the stars were aligned for the tour of the planets, they're also aligned for this really magical, special thing that's happening for humankind.”For Fran Bagenal, a planetary scientist at the University of Colorado, Boulder, who began working with Voyager 1 as a graduate student during its earliest years, the occasion is a momentous technological feat. “What's exciting is the fact that we have a spacecraft that was built in the mid ’70s that is still working,” she says. “Storing data on an eight-track tape that’s working on a spacecraft after 50 years—I mean, it’s amazing.”Even as Voyager 1 approaches its 50-year anniversary next September, and its end of mission perhaps not long after that, the spacecraft is still checking items off its laundry list of scientific achievements. The spacecraft—alongside its twin, Voyager 2—was originally intended to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment to observe the outer planets.But Voyager 1 kept traveling beyond the solar system and is now exploring the interstellar medium that fills the space between star systems. Voyager 1’s remoteness gives researchers a rare opportunity to study how the effects of the sun ripple even into the interstellar medium—and at what point those effects wane, says Jamie Rankin, deputy project scientist for the Voyager Mission at Princeton University.Just as both Voyager spacecraft are moving through space, so is our own solar system—only about 35,000 miles per hour slower, Badaruddin says. That means that as the pair continue their journeys, they’re sending back information about the space that our own sun and planet will pass through in about three years’ time.“We can learn from telescopes and Earth-orbiting observatories, but there's really nothing like having a spacecraft in that environment that's sending us data,” Badaruddin says.Courtesy of NASA/JPL-CaltechVoyager 1’s unprecedented journey isn’t without challenges. The craft has stayed in communication with Earth far longer than planned and is trekking through regions of space that it was never built to encounter or study. Researchers are helping maintain crucial functions, but they’re now doing so with a full day of lag in communications both to and from the spacecraft, Badaruddin says.“Light time is really affecting us,” he says. “You factor it in. It’s like having a long commute.” Building new commands for the spacecraft is now a week-long process, for instance, since it takes time to receive data from the spacecraft, analyze it, and create a new command, he adds.Still, the Voyager team is used to navigating unforeseen circumstances. For decades, they’ve been managing to make do with a dwindling power supply coming from the craft’s nuclear generators. In September, mission operations switched off some of Voyager 1’s devices in lieu of lower-power alternatives, a maneuver the team dubbed the “Big Bang.” The swap, which saved the craft 10 watts of power, kept mission operations from having to switch off another instrument as early as next summer.Courtesy of NASA/JPL-CaltechEven when contact with Voyager 1 is eventually lost, the spacecraft will leave a lasting legacy—especially for any future such far-traveling missions, should NASA or another space agency launch one. A successor to Voyager might, for instance, have new devices such as a dust instrument to better analyze the interstellar medium or cameras to give astronomers a better view of these distant stretches of the cosmos, Rankin says.“I would hope that the Voyagers and their reaching interstellar space has taught us the lesson that we've got to just keep reaching for the stars,” she adds.Every mission must meet its end, though. And Badaruddin’s best guess is that Voyager 1’s could come in the next three to five years, as the plutonium-238 powering it decays further. Once the craft transmits its final signal to Earth, it will still continue its silent tour of the galaxy.But Badaruddin acknowledges he’s part of a lineage of mission managers who have said that the spacecraft only has a few years left, only to be proven wrong. “The Big Bang was a rabbit we pulled out of a hat. As long as we can keep finding rabbits, we can keep going,” he says. “Don’t bet against Voyager.”

schema.headline: Voyager 1 Beat the Odds and Is Still Working a Light-Day Away From Earth

title: America’s AI Chip War Is Heating Up in the Dumbest Possible Ways
description: This week, the Trump administration made it significantly harder for Chinese companies to access some of the world’s most advanced AI chips. For years
body: This week, the Trump administration made it significantly harder for Chinese companies to access some of the world’s most advanced AI chips. For years, tech firms like Alibaba and ByteDance could rent computing power from data centers overseas, allowing them to use powerful Nvidia chips they were generally prohibited from physically importing into China. This is known as remote access.But under new plans announced on Monday, overseas data centers that want to provide large amounts of computing power to China will have to get special licenses and deal with other annoying new kinds of red tape. The White House also imposed stricter rules on shipments of advanced chips to five countries, including Singapore and Malaysia, where US officials suspect significant levels of smuggling may have taken place.These are not new policy ideas, and similar proposals have been kicking around in Washington for a while. But the timing of Monday’s announcement is impossible to ignore. Yes, this is about Jensen Huang’s sex life.As you’ve probably heard by now, the Nvidia cofounder resigned as CEO last week after admitting he had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence services. Alice previously worked at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which offered remote access services and is suspected of engaging in chip smuggling.The scandal may have been so embarrassing for the White House that officials felt compelled to demonstrate they had the situation under control. Apparently, the cheating scandal of the century was the motivation they were missing. (A White House spokesperson previously told WIRED that the new rule would “crack down on the smuggling of advanced US SI chips” and “help ensure that America’s most advanced chips go first to US SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies.”)It started in the fall of 2022, when the Biden administration unveiled a set of rules that would radically alter the future of AI and who was allowed to build it. The goal was to choke off China's access to the advanced chips needed to train the world's most powerful AI models, as well as the equipment required to manufacture those chips.It's worth remembering just how radical this approach was at the time. For decades, the US had used export controls to keep sensitive American technology away from specific military programs, governments, and blacklisted companies accused of carrying out human rights abuses. But the Biden administration was attempting something far more ambitious: using Washington's influence over the global semiconductor industry to hold back the world's second-largest economy from competing at the cutting edge of one of the most important new technologies in generations.The strategy rested on a relatively simple idea. Training the most advanced AI models requires enormous amounts of computing power, and American companies like Nvidia dominate the market for the chips that provide it. By restricting China's access to those chips, Washington hoped to preserve America's technological lead.Four years later, the US certainly cannot claim total victory. But boy, have things gotten messy. Part of the problem is that Washington tasked the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), a relatively small, underfunded agency within the Commerce Department, with leading enforcement of the controls. The bureau had a budget of just $235 million in 2026—a paltry sum compared to what Nvidia rakes in in a single week.The bureau's job only got harder as the Biden administration introduced successive rounds of increasingly complex restrictions, scrambling to tighten the rules as chipmakers found increasingly elaborate ways to get around them. But one of the bureau's biggest challenges was fighting what became a booming industry for smuggling AI chips into China.At BIS, Megaspeed has become a poster child for the problem, although it's far from the only company suspected of involvement, or even the largest, according to a person familiar with the matter.According to Bloomberg, roughly 50,000 of the estimated 136,000 AI chips Megaspeed imported into Malaysia and Indonesia in 2024 and 2025 weren't accounted for in Nvidia's initial inventory checks. It's not clear where they may have ended up. (Nvidia later said it had found at least some of them.)Even if all of the unaccounted-for chips ended up in China, they would represent only a fraction of the advanced semiconductors believed to have been smuggled into the country over the past few years. Researchers at the Institute for Progress estimate that, by the end of 2026, China could have accumulated smuggled computing power equivalent to roughly 1 million of Nvidia's high-end H100 chips.But all along, Chinese companies didn't necessarily need to smuggle chips into the country to use them. They could just rent computing power from data centers in other countries, and best of all, the practice didn’t violate US export controls. This wasn’t some hidden loophole—every policymaker and researcher who worked on the chip restrictions was deeply aware of it. So why let the practice continue?For one, renting computing power can be more expensive and cumbersome than owning the chips outright, especially for companies that need to train large AI models over long periods. Some analysts argued that allowing Chinese firms to use American technology overseas could help keep them dependent on it instead of pushing them to develop domestic alternatives. Restricting access would also be difficult to enforce and could hurt US technology companies.Now, Washington is moving into this territory anyway. Monday's announcement represents another significant expansion of US efforts to control China's technological development. In 2022, Washington set out to prevent Chinese companies from acquiring certain American chips. Four years later, it’s trying to regulate how Chinese companies use those same chips, even when the hardware never enters China.Whether that's a good idea depends partly on how much the original restrictions have actually accomplished.There is evidence that export controls have made it considerably harder for Chinese AI companies to acquire the kind of computing power of their American competitors. But assessing the precise impact of the policies has proven to be extremely difficult.This strategy comes with a lot of risks, and like with everything else in life, there are real winners and losers. For example, forcing US chip companies to cut off Chinese customers has come at a cost to American companies. In a study of earlier US export restrictions, researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that affected American suppliers struggled to replace lost business in China with new customers elsewhere. They estimate that the restrictions wiped $130 billion from the companies’ combined market value, while also hurting their profitability and employment.The restrictions have also given China a very powerful incentive to find ways to compete in AI without relying on American technology. Huawei, for example, developed a way to link powerful chips together to create larger, more powerful megachip systems. The Chinese AI lab DeepSeek proved to the world that finding ways to make training more efficient could help developers build competitive models with fewer resources.I worry that the Trump administration will soon find that it has gotten out over its own skis. It’s now trying to control not only which chips Chinese companies can buy from American companies, but also how they can use American technology anywhere it may be in the world. I’m not sure that is the kind of responsibility I want to bestow on anyone in response to what happened in one person’s sex life.This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

schema.headline: America’s AI Chip War Is Heating Up in the Dumbest Possible Ways

title: Top Maytag Promo Codes: 15% Off
description: The Maytag Man is one of the most enduring characters in American advertising, lonely because no one needs his help repairing a Maytag appliance. The
body: The Maytag Man is one of the most enduring characters in American advertising, lonely because no one needs his help repairing a Maytag appliance. The Maytag brand, too, has endured—dating back to the days when Frederick Maytag’s washers used wooden tubs and cranks. Maytag was the first company to put an agitator at the bottom of a washing machine, a design still in use today. It was also the first to stack a washer and dryer and one of the earliest adopters of smart appliances. But mostly, the brand has eschewed novelty and staked its claim on durability and reliability for its heavy-duty dishwashers, washers, dryers, refrigerators, and ovens. This is true even as Maytag came under the ownership of former competitor Whirlpool.Maytag remains one of the few appliance companies to offer 10-year limited warranties on essential parts. But Maytag promo codes are more ephemeral, offering short-term deals on appliances that will hopefully last a decade. Here’s how to get a Maytag coupon code and Maytag promo codes, and to find closeout deals on last season’s Maytag appliances to save even more.Save Big With Maytag Appliance Closeout DealsA simple way to find discounts on Maytag appliances is to check out overstock and closeout deals, which feature substantial markdowns on last season’s models as Maytag clears space for new products. These deals don't need a coupon code but do require knowing the right place to look. Visit the Maytag outlet website for appliance closeout offers. Usually, these deals are available only until supplies last.Select Customers Can Get a Special Maytag Promo CodeLike many big companies, Maytag offers professional discounts for military, first responders, health care workers, students, and teachers. To receive up to a 15% discount as an active military member, veteran, or spouse, you’ll need to create a Maytag account and verify your military status through the SheerID program. Maytag first responder and health care worker discounts also require SheerID verification. There’s also a discount program for students and teachers, including a teacher savings program and up to 15% off sitewide. Verified students can access student-specific pricing when moving into their first off-campus apartment.Work Smarter, Not Harder With Maytag Smart AppliancesMaytag is also offering deals on select smart appliances. This includes a unique combination toaster-microwave that’s about $100 off MSRP, and a slide-in electric range with smart connectivity that’s steeply discounted to $1,260—hundreds of dollars less than even other recent sale prices. You can check out the special Maytag deals on connected and smart appliances by scrolling to the bottom of Maytag’s smart appliance page.

title: The Dark Side of the Moon Was the Brightest Part of 2026
description: Astronauts have a well-deserved reputation for being focused on their work. After spending years preparing for a single mission, they’re all business
body: Astronauts have a well-deserved reputation for being focused on their work. After spending years preparing for a single mission, they’re all business as they hurtle through the cosmos, ever vigilant that a brief lapse in concentration can mean catastrophe. That mindset is a big reason why the crew of NASA’s Artemis II was so oblivious to their celebrity as they circumnavigated the moon in April. It wasn’t until the seventh day of their nearly 10-day journey that they began to realize their exploits were causing a massive stir back home.“We were talking to our families for the second time,” recalls Jeremy Hansen, the sole Canadian in the four-person crew. “And that’s when we all heard, one after another: ‘Hey, this is really resonating on the planet in a way that you’re going to be shocked by.’”Hansen and his comrades were overwhelmed by their fame once they splashed back down on Earth. Nearly 150 million people had watched the mission’s key moments on NASA’s online platforms, which included feeds with near-constant access to the interior of the Orion spacecraft. The buzz around the mission harkened back to the glory days of American spaceflight, when people would gather around TV sets to marvel at astronauts floating outside their capsules or bounding around the moon.The romantic spirit of the Artemis program’s long-term objective certainly helped: People are alive to the dream of a moon base that’s meant to serve our species’ idealistic aspirations rather than be a zillionaire’s private plaything. Artemis II supported that noble mission by putting the Orion’s life-support, navigation, and piloting systems through their paces. But fans were also drawn to the crew’s infectious energy. There was palpable chemistry between Hansen, Christina Koch, Victor Glover, and Reid Wiseman, all of whom exuded pure joy and wonder as they dealt with the minutiae of life aboard a multibillion-dollar vehicle traveling as fast as 25,000 miles per hour.“It was not a natural thing for us,” admits Hansen. “You have four type-A personalities who are willing to strap themselves to a rocket and go to the moon. We were doing stuff for the first time, and it was not uncommon for us to have four different opinions.” When the astronauts began to notice that interpersonal friction was becoming problematic during training, they enlisted the aid of professionals. During a September 2024 training trip to Iceland, the crew spent two extra days in conversations and teamwork exercises organized by Rick Rochelle, a renowned leadership guru. Once the Artemis II schedule was firmed up, the crew made a pact: Launch as friends, land as friends.Their historic flight past the far side of the moon marked the apex of that friendship. They were more than 250,000 miles away from Earth. The planet looked no bigger than a fingernail sliver—“just this lifeboat hanging undisturbingly in the universe,” Koch would later say during the crew’s first public remarks after touchdown. “You look at it, and you just kind of shake your head,” says Hansen. “How can we do anything other than lift one another up and try to make life better for one another?”Then that “tiny Earth” vanished as the spacecraft went behind the moon, and the crew spent 40 minutes out of radio contact. They carved out a few seconds to toast each other with maple cookies—carefully, to keep crumbs from floating free in zero gravity. They also selected a crater to name for Wiseman’s late wife, Carroll, who died of cancer in 2020. Soon after they reemerged from total isolation, they came together in an ecstatic, four-person embrace. “I knew right there that we were going to be bound together for life,” Wiseman says.There were plenty of lowlights during the mission, too. Some lint got trapped in the primary urine vent line, Wiseman says, “so we had to go to a backup method of urination, which for the men wasn’t bad, but for the woman wasn’t great.” Another hiccup involved a smoke detector that erroneously went off while the spacecraft was still 80,000 miles from home, leading to 15 minutes of intense anxiety.None of the Artemis II crew members are likely to return to space: Hansen, Glover, and Wiseman have all moved on from astronaut life, and Koch transitioned into a leadership role at NASA. Their new, less stressful lives should give them ample opportunity to cheer on Artemis III, tentatively scheduled to launch in summer 2027—an event that may once again remind us that we’re all part of a shared story far bigger than ourselves.What did we miss? Tell us about your favorite moments of 2026 in the comments below.

schema.headline: The Dark Side of the Moon Was the Brightest Part of 2026

title: The US Lost Its Measles Elimination Status. It’ll Take Years to Get It Back
description: The US has hit terrible twin milestones over the past week: Two more people died from measles, bringing this year’s death count to double digits, and
body: The US has hit terrible twin milestones over the past week: Two more people died from measles, bringing this year’s death count to double digits, and the country officially lost its status as a country that had eliminated the highly infectious disease.The US eliminated measles in 2000 and maintained that status for 26 years. Now, the nation faces an uphill battle to vanquish the virus once more, and it will take years to be measles-free again.Noel Brewer, a professor of health behavior at the University of North Carolina, presented a report last week to the Pan American Health Organization showing continuous measles transmission for at least 12 months in the US—erasing one of the nation’s greatest public health achievements.WIRED asked him how he felt after PAHO officials reached a consensus that the country was no longer measles-free. He paused.“I have not actually thought about my reaction,” he says. After a beat, he says that the loss is “a somber moment for public health” that’s particularly wrenching because it’s a “completely avoidable situation.” Mexico and Canada have managed to wind down their outbreaks, but “measles in America is a runaway train,” Brewer says. “There's no end in sight, and it may even be gaining speed.”PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa da Silva Jr. officially announced the change in status on Tuesday. “Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” he said at a press conference. “It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization, and death.” Bolivia and Mexico also lost their elimination status this year; Canada lost it a year ago.Brewer presented three key lines of evidence showing that measles has become endemic in the US. The outbreak in Utah and Arizona has gone on for more than 12 months, and the US has had measles cases every week since January 20, 2025. The genomic data also shows a great deal of similarity across states, indicating the clusters are closely linked—and each week, there are cases where the sources can’t be confirmed, indicating they didn’t come from travel or known contact with other patients.“We have a problem on our hands,” says William Moss, epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins. And it’s not going away anytime soon. To reclaim its status as measles-free, the US will have to prove it has gone a full year without continued transmission. That’s unlikely to happen under the Trump administration—and its actions have made it more difficult for future leaders.“Reestablishing elimination is not just about reporting fewer cases—it also requires convincing the world that we have a strong enough surveillance system to find cases and deaths,” Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiologist and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University, tells WIRED in a text.The fact that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and state health departments differ on how many people have died from measles “is a sign of dysfunction,” Nuzzo says. There have been 10 confirmed measles deaths so far this year—seven in Pennsylvania, two in Wisconsin, and one in New York—but the CDC only lists six.Such chaos also breeds distrust, says Frederic Bertley, president and CEO of the Center of Science and Industry. That's “a huge problem” for a public trying to parse who is telling the truth and whether they should listen, he says.Even as measles was eliminated, anti-vaccine rhetoric began to rise, especially around the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine. Vaccination rates began falling—spurred in part by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an environmental lawyer turned anti-vaccine activist who published a now-retracted article alleging a link between vaccines and autism in 2005. He continued crusading against vaccines as head of Children’s Health Defense and at the helm of the Department of Health and Human Services during President Donald Trump’s second term.The Trump administration has done little to stop the outbreaks, cutting billions in funding from state, local, territorial, and tribal public health departments and offering conflicting messages on vaccines. During a televised February 2025 cabinet meeting following the first child death in a decade, Kennedy said “it's not unusual, we have measles outbreaks every year.” The CDC hasn’t held a single press conference on measles throughout the entire outbreak; as PAHO was making its measles status announcement on Tuesday, HHS sent out an email about Kennedy’s cooking show.“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC director Erica Schwartz said in a statement. “Losing a designation doesn't mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.” Kennedy posted on X, “I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”To regain its elimination status, the US needs to address barriers to health care access, missed vaccination opportunities, misinformation, and vaccine hesitancy, Barbosa said. That includes mounting wide-reaching vaccination campaigns, expanding laboratory testing capacity, and responding quickly to cases, including contact tracing. It’s the bread and butter of public health, but the longer it takes to create a comprehensive response, the more it will cost, experts warn.Future efforts to contain measles will require “a stronger centralized federal response to these outbreaks” paired with support for “very local responses,” says Moss. That means identifying communities with long-standing under-vaccination and understanding why, he says, as well as improving trust in public health guidance.“Immunity gaps” tend to concentrate in specific geographic areas and communities, and national or even state-level data can “mask these significant inequalities, providing an incomplete picture of the population's actual level of protection,” Barbosa said.The CDC announced $100 million in August and September—more than a year after the outbreak began—to help fund state and regional efforts to combat measles, but Congress will need to allocate $100 million to $400 million more for measles elimination in coming months, Brewer says.“More than 90 percent of children get the measles vaccine, Brewer points out. “This is a vaccine that has extraordinary public support, and it goes across the aisle.”But to achieve herd immunity, vaccination rates need to be at least 95 percent due to how contagious the disease is. High transmissibility also means measles is very hard to uproot once it begins to spread.Yet ending national measles transmission is “its own reward,” Brewer says. It spares children’s lives, keeps them out of hospitals, and prevents blindness and other lifelong complications. “We no longer have that benefit,” he says. “Children are now being stalked by this incurable and deadly disease.”

schema.headline: The US Lost Its Measles Elimination Status. It’ll Take Years to Get It Back

title: Inside Nvidia’s First Post-Jensen All-Hands: Pay Raises and More Equity
description: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress made her first address to the staff on Wednesday and just minutes into the meeting told employees that they can expec
body: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress made her first address to the staff on Wednesday and just minutes into the meeting told employees that they can expect pay raises and more equity in December, months ahead of schedule, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED.“So I’m here to tell you, the best thing that we want to do is to take care of each and every single employee that is here and to make sure that you feel good about this company and you do not worry about your comp,” she said.Questions about compensation were the most common among the 700 submitted ahead of the meeting, Kress said. She said the next-most common request was for transparency from the board.Kress’ comments came during the first companywide meeting following the resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO last week. Huang had led the computer graphics chip maker since cofounding it 33 years ago, and his presentations during the quarterly town halls internally had become a much anticipated and memorable spectacle for some of the company’s nearly 49,000 employees. Information rarely leaked from the meetings in the past. Nvidia declined to comment for this story.But now Nvidia is facing an extraordinary leadership crisis. Huang resigned amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including potentially with a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia’s board chair Harvey Jones said on Tuesday that Huang disclosed “personal behavior” contrary to the company’s policies and norms and wouldn’t be invited back.During the companywide meeting on Wednesday, Jones reiterated that the board accepted Huang’s resignation due to his personal conduct and “lack of candor.” He said the company wouldn’t find a “Jensen clone,” but that there are “dynamic leaders out there, with demonstrated intellect, high-tech engineering experience, strategic thinking, cultural compatibility, and a track record of success.” He added, “We will not compromise our requirements for the sake of expediency” and that the board would accept employee suggestions on the CEO search.Got a Tip?Are you a current or former Nvidia employee who wants to talk about what’s happening? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporters securely on Signal at ChaoticGoode.12 and peard33.24.Thousands of employees have apparently lobbied for Huang’s reinstatement. Several well-known tech executives signed a public petition, with about 200,000 purported backers urging the same. Instead, the board is searching internally and externally for a replacement at one of the world’s most valuable companies and one of the biggest drivers of the generative AI boom.Huang’s departures and a slew of government investigations into him and Nvidia have rattled investors. But on Tuesday, Nvidia reported better-than-expected financial results and forecast growing sales in the years to come. Shares were up about 5 percent on Wednesday.One concern investors have expressed is whether Nvidia might see a brain drain of top talent. Many employees have stayed at Nvidia for Huang and his vision. Nvidia could also be perceived as a less desirable place for new and emerging talent to work, with its leadership in flux, during an especially critical time as competition in the AI chips market grows.On Tuesday’s third-quarter earnings call, an analyst from Bank of America Securities asked Kress directly about her “message” to Nvidia investors about talent retention, as well as the company’s overall durability and financial strategy through this major upheaval. Kress replied that “probably the most important thing” company leaders are thinking through right now is stabilizing its employee ranks.“We are always thinking about our employees. Like every community out there, there are diverse opinions,” Kress said. “We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure they are safe and make sure the work can be done in the current environment.”In a brief question-and-answer session with Kress during the all-hands meeting Wednesday, Nvidia cofounder Chris Malachowsky addressed how the company could maintain its prized culture going forward.He recalled how he, Huang, and other cofounders thought it was “nonsense” to put cultural values up on posters. Instead, they want it instilled in “the way you behave, the way you work together, and the way you work,” and he believes that will stand the test of time. “We’re going to be fine,” he said.Kress ended the meeting, which lasted about 50 minutes, by comparing Nvidia’s employees to “90,000 people packed into the sweatiest, hottest” University of Florida football game.In the third quarter, “every single person sings,” she said. “It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony singing that song … Do you know what? We’re gonna hear that song, guys. And I believe in all of you, that you will help sing it. Nvidia, we’ve got this.”Updated: 11/18/2026 1:26 p.m. EST: Updated with new details on comments made during the Nvidia all-hands meeting.

schema.headline: Inside Nvidia’s First Post-Jensen All-Hands: Pay Raises and More Equity

title: Jensen Huang Says He’s Open to Coming Back to Nvidia
description: Jensen Huang said that he is open to returning as chief executive of Nvidia, five days after he resigned from the company.In a statement published Tue
body: Jensen Huang said that he is open to returning as chief executive of Nvidia, five days after he resigned from the company.In a statement published Tuesday morning on X, Huang said that since stepping down he has received an “outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.”“If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote.Huang also thanked people who showed “kindness” to him and his family and acknowledged “the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met.” He reiterated his love for America and Nvidia and his remorse for his unfaithfulness to his wife, which he also expressed in a company-wide email sent last week.Huang resigned four days after Nvidia launched an internal investigation into an affair he had admitted to having with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who has no known relation to Jensen. Huang reportedly misled the company’s general counsel and chief marketing officer about the affair with Alice.The day before Huang stepped down, The New York Times reported that he'd had a second affair with one of his direct reports at Nvidia. After his resignation, Reuters reported on an alleged third affair with another Nvidia employee. The company’s code of conduct discourages "personal relationships" that "may create a conflict of interest."Colette Kress, Nvidia’s longtime chief financial officer, was installed as interim CEO upon Huang’s resignation.The New York Times first reported Jensen’s association with Alice, also known as Huang Le, in October 2025. On November 6 of this year, citing an intelligence memo that reportedly circulated among Trump administration officials last spring, The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that intelligence officials believed Alice may be an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump administration officials, including tech executive and White House Science and Technology advisory council cochair David Sacks, have questioned whether Alice was associated with the MSS. The Chinese government has rejected claims that Alice spied for the nation.WIRED reported last week that on the same day Huang resigned, Nvidia employees began using an existing petition to the board to call for his reinstatement. It gained more than 1,600 comments in just a few hours.A separate, public petition titled “Stand With Jensen” similarly calls for the executive’s return. At the time of writing, it has more than 193,000 online signatures, including more than 11,000 self-identified current and former Nvidia employees and more than 100,000 self-identified shareholders. On Friday, Elon Musk said that he was going to sign the petition, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan claimed that he had signed.President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he “would not mind” if Huang returned as CEO, adding that he believed Huang had “learned a big lesson.”Nvidia’s board of directors, however, reportedly said on Monday that it was not considering reinstating Huang as CEO. On Tuesday, the board announced that it had established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee “for board-level oversight of the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.”

schema.headline: Jensen Huang Says He’s Open to Coming Back to Nvidia
